anh_en: She's always so serious, following every rule despite being our de facto leader now. Well, she's taken care of me before on many occasions, so I gotta show some respect... Wait, I've been a Bloom Bearer for years? How time flies…

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Aalto's a master at mind games. It's hard to get under his skin! He's not strong enough to pique my interest though. That guy relies on trickery too much for my liking.

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: The Loong Maiden of <te href=850091>Jinzhou</te> reminds me of the Shorekeeper, the way they're oh-so-devoted to their duties, all the self-sacrifice! I don't understand, why must they burden themselves so much?

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: That girl, the Taoist? She's a fun one to watch. She may seem to follow human society's boring norms, but her untamed spirit still shines through every now and then.

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Your birthday is the most wonderful day. Without you, my life would be so empty and dull! Being with you again brings me peace. I am content now. Hey, put your Terminal away, great savior of <te href=850079>Solaris</te>! I blocked all signals here so we can be undisturbed. Today, you're mine, and no one else's.

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Hehe... How do you like this flower?

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Camellya, a Bloom Bearer of <te href=850109>the Black Shores</te>. Happy to see you again! My beloved... seed of fate.

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Hehe... I'm looking forward to our game.

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Where are you, my lovely seeds?

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Ahh... I love it... The power surging through my veins...!

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Oops, watch out for my thorns. Don't get your fingers pierced. Hmm... on second thought, not much can harm you anyway.

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Hey, care to join me for another round? I'll show you a whole bunch of new tricks and powers, promise!

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: ...Ugh! Hah... I-I'm fine, I just... need some time, to ride out the pain... Swallow it whole, make the chaotic frequencies my strength...

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: With this power, I am whole again... Now we can truly play as equals. After all, it's not just what you play... but who you play with. Don't you agree?

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: Don't run, keep the dance going!

speaker: Camellya
anh_en: The lovely smell of all my prey...

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: I'm always on the go, collecting treasures, helping my friends, making costumes, and repairing stage props... It's a busy routine, but seeing everyone smiling makes it all worth it.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: <te href=850122>Pero</te>'s box is more than just a treasure trove. It's my private lounge as well. It's bigger than you might think, and I've stashed all my nifty gadgets inside. Would you like a tour? Knock, knock—open up, Pero.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Apparently, the mix of my over-the-top gestures and stoic face is hilarious to people. See? Just like that. Oh, did I actually get a chuckle out of you? Guess I'll keep this style going, then.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Our troupe never lets anyone feel left out. We accept everyone, chasing away their worries and inviting them to be a part of the performance. If you ever feel down or sad, come see us. I'd really like to see you smile.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: People say family is about helping and comforting each other. I feel safe and warm around you... So, maybe you count as family after all?

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: I like turning the things I collect into stage props. They might not look fancy at first, but each one has its own special story. On stage, the ordinary becomes extraordinary, and I think that's worth something.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Cleaning up the ship is always a headache. There's algae, sewage spills, and torn canvas everywhere... And of course, there's always that person who conveniently disappears when it's time to pitch in. Pft, not like a good living and performance space is important or anything. You agree, right?

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Spaghetti Bolognese is great on its own, but it's even better when shared. Maybe... it's the company that makes it taste better?

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Every time I see the mess those drunkards leave behind... Ugh, I just want to dump all the booze into the ocean.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: One day, the streets of <te href=850097>Ragunna</te> will be alive with the spirit of freedom. Until then, I want it to grow within our troupe. We'll make the sad smile, help the hopeless dream again, give courage to the fearful, and remind everyone of who we really are.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: <te href=850122>Pero</te> is my best friend. She's amazing. She can detect special frequencies on objects, carry all my stuff, and even absorb good and bad feelings and inspirations. But don't worry, she won't gobble up anything harmful, dangerous, or anything that belongs to someone.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Luceanite pebbles, if not collected in time, will lose their glow and turn to dust. I used to be one of those lost pebbles, until the <te href=850108>Troupe of Fools</te> came along and saved me. Now, I can help other lost souls with my own little light.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Brant is the greatest captain in all of Solaris. At least, that's what he insists I say. But it's true, having him around really does bring out the best in us. His passion is infectious, and his belief in freedom is like the mast that keeps us all steady.

speaker: Roccia
anh_en: Leading a large family is like steering a massive ship. It requires immense effort to keep it on course. I have firsthand experience in managing a vessel, and I admire her energy and bravery in navigating this journey.

speaker: Roccia

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: Would you care to know why the musical structure of this performance intrigues me so? The massive Ferris wheel I saw to the west side of Skob. Two cabins, locked in a perfect chase, forever parallel, much like a perfect fugue. They are bound to cross paths again, perhaps yearning to draw closer, yet forever unable to touch... How about joining in and becoming a part of this silent piece?

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: The winds of Dolores are more brisk than I imagined. Their bite mirrors the audience's stoic silence, both filled with tension. From the conductor's podium, I can almost hear the wind whispering. It's as if I've stepped outside myself. I stand there, letting the wind scatter my hair. It blows away thoughts I shouldn't have... and maybe even me. Hmm, maybe that concert hall owner was right, and I've gone a bit mad.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: I've said it all now... Don't overthink it. These words have been waiting to be spoken for a long time. speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: I control the phrasing and dynamic balance through the rise and fall of my hands, shaping the notes into the sounds I desire. speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: After enough failures, the sting fades, and with it, the burden of worry.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: The taste of redcurrants... the only thing that has left an impression on me. Its sour and bitter taste, perhaps? I find it quite tolerable actually. Maybe I've simply grown used to it...

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: After meat is smoked or roasted, its taste is similar to... Never mind.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: I wish to comprehend the cycle of life by experiencing it over and over again.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: Hecate has always stood at the crossroads of the <te href=851026>other world</te>, waiting, as if knowing that our paths would inevitably meet. Only when I placed my hand in its palm did I realize—Hecate is me. The me of the other world, the me of this world, and the me who moves freely between them... From that moment on, "I" became the guardian of the boundary, perceiving all, seeing even the farthest reaches of both worlds.

speaker: Phrolova

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: Your birthday? Today, you say? Oh.\n…\nWell, if you're expecting a present or some kind wishes, then simply wait here. A long wait can be considered a gift in itself.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: Do not fear the Fractsidus Overseer. Settle your mind. Quiet the clamor of thought. Only then can you stay and truly appreciate the perfect melody echoing through the Lycoris sea... and the true paradise that is soon to arrive.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: Come, let us finish this performance we've all been waiting for. Together.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: See? I haven't lost my touch.

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: The warm yet bittersweet first movement is hidden in the dark night, alone and forlorn. Now, those haunting, ghostly cries have begun to fade away.

speaker: Phrolova

speaker: Phrolova

speaker: Phrolova

speaker: Phrolova
anh_en: Will the approaching sounds be... beautiful enough?

Ever since she was a child, Suisui loved collecting beautiful trinkets. Whether it was a dyed feather or a gleaming gemstone, everything found a home in her little treasure box. Over time, her collection grew into a glittering hoard of jade and jewelry, which she took endless delight in using to dress up Yangyang.

Among all of them, her absolute favorite remained the green jade pendant gifted by her parents. The jade was as warm and smooth as gentle water, carved into the shape of a bird poised to take flight at any moment.

"Wear this jade close to your heart, and let your spirit soar. May you spread your wings like the Chongming bird, with eyes unclouded, and a path always clear before you."

A folding fan crafted by the finest artisans of Mengzhou. Its face features a landscape embroidered with ultra-fine gold and emerald threads. Distant mountains rise like dark jade, mist hovers over the nearby waters, and a few koi fish swim leisurely through river weed. It is a masterpiece of breathtaking beauty.

The year Suisui took charge of the Commerce Guild, a massive crisis threatened to collapse everything she had built. Competitors pooled their pressure, and allies turned their backs one by one. Trapped in her study for three whole days, she was on the verge of signing the file of surrender. But on the fourth morning, as she pushed open the window for air, her eyes fell upon this old fan resting on her desk. She remembered buying it with the very first gold she had ever earned, back when her younger self declared she would "hold the rivers and mountains in the palm of my hand." Gripping the fan, Suisui channeled her Forte into it. Watching the embroidered ripples slowly stir to life, her chaotic thoughts finally settled.

Eventually, she overcame that crisis. From that day on, she kept the fan by her side, its face alive with silver waves, soaring birds, and swimming fish. Looking at the scenery, it was as if she were gazing upon her favorite view of all: a world at peace.

When Suisui was twelve, she and Yangyang used fresh peach-blossom juice to dye two stacks of letter paper. Holding her brush with utmost care, Suisui drew a pair of little birds snuggling in the corner of the paper. The right one was herself, and the left was her little sister.

Years later, Yangyang left for Jinzhou to become an Outrider, while Suisui continued her travels as a businesswoman. They kept in touch through letters, and Suisui carefully folded every message from her sister, keeping them tucked inside her letter stack.

Years have passed, and the paper has long since run out. Unable to bring herself to use the very last blank sheet, Suisui keeps it safely on her study desk. The two snuggling birds in the corner have faded with time, smoothed over by countless tender touches. Yet, every time she pulls out her sister's letters to read, she feels that no matter how many miles separate them, those two clumsy, crooked little birds are still holding each other tight.

Yangyang's hair ribbon and hat. The ribbon was a parting blessing from her mother; the hat, a gift from her friends after she became an <te href=850139>Outrider</te>. She wants now to stride boldly forward, to open her wings to the sky. Her wishes have already drifted on the wind to every corner of the world, and so she means to anchor a new self, an "adult" who can carry others' burdens, an azure-plumed bird winging in the high heavens, heralding the dawn.

Spring days lingered, slow and sweet. In a Mingting's courtyard, the flowers were in magnificent bloom.

Suisui sat slumped over her desk, a brush clutched in her hand and a smudge of orcher paint on her cheek. After painting intently for hours, she stood up to admire her masterpiece—a cluster of overlapping blues, greens, and deep reds. It was hard to tell what it was, but it radiated a cozy warmth. Content with her work, Suisui snatched the paper and dashed outside.

"Yangyang! Yangyang—"

In a flash, the paper was in Yangyang's hands. Suisui leaned against the qin table, staring at her sister. "Can you tell what it is?" 
Yangyang studied it, her fingertip tapping a golden smudge on the right, then a white one on the left. "It's... two little birds, snuggling together." 
Suisui's eyes lit up, and she smacked the table. "Exactly! They're birds! I knew those adults were blind! They kept saying they were baby chicks!"
"No, they aren't," Yangyang put the drawing down and tilted her head. "A baby chick's tail droops. These are perked up."
"That's right!" Suisui wanted nothing more than to scoop her sister up and spin her around. "Only you understand my art!"
Despite the high praise, Yangyang just offered a gentle smile. She pointed to the golden cluster on the right. "Is this one you, Sister?"
"Mm-hmm! The right one is me, and the left one is you." Suisui leaned closer, using the tail end of her paintbrush to point at the snowy bird. "See? It's dainty. Just like you."

That was how the springs of their childhood slipped by. Outside, clusters of pink and white blossoms weighed heavily against green leaves. Whenever a breeze swept through, petals would drift onto the qin table, the girls' sketches, and their hair. Soft sunlight bathed the courtyard in golden hue. Birds chirped beneath the eaves, blending with the drifting notes of Yangyang's qin. Suisui would laze on the veranda, holding her drawing high against the sky to watch the colors bleed through the paper.

Days moved so slowly back then. The shadows moved forward inch by inch, carrying away whole afternoons. And then, before one could realize, many springs had already passed by.

Once summer arrived, the courtyard felt as suffocating as a large bamboo steamer.

The ceaseless song of cicadas swelled from dawn till dusk. Even the lotus flowers in the water vat under the eaves hung limp, mirroring Suisui's exact mood. She lay slumped across the windowsill, staring out at the sun-bleached sky. Behind her, Yangyang sat practicing her qin. She had replayed the same melody seven or eight times, its notes melting in the dense heat. Listening to it, Suisui felt as though her own brain was about to dissolve into a puddle just like the music.

"Are you going out, Sister?" Yangyang paused, hearing her push herself up.
"To the river," Suisui tossed a smile back over her shoulder, her long hair whipping past her jacket. "There's a breeze over there. I'm stifling to death inside."
"But the sun is blinding—"
"It won't kill me!" Her voice was already vanishing around the corner of the wall.

The riverbank wasn't far, just a quick dash through two alleys. Suisui walked briskly, knocking her folding fan rhythmically against her palm. The moment she stepped onto the embankment, a cool, damp breeze greeted her, thick with the fragrance of river reeds. 

The docks were a bustling hive of activity. At a nearby stall, a middle-aged merchant was clacking away on an abacus, calling out numbers line by line as the beads flew. Mesmerized, Suisui stepped closer, her lips moving in a silent murmur as she mentally kept count alongside him.

As the merchant snapped the final bead into place and looked up, he gasped, startled by her bright, intensely focused eyes. "Where did you spring from, little girl?"
"Manager Liu, that's three hundred and twenty-seven bolts of fabric in total, right?" Suisui chimed in, ignoring his question entirely.
Manager Liu looked from his ledger to her, a smile tugging beneath his mustache. "You were following my abacus?"
"Didn't need to. I did the mental math while you were reading the numbers aloud," Suisui grinned, completely unfazed. "And that batch of tea leaves was one hundred and six and a half jin, wasn't it? I caught a snippet of it while walking past."
Manager Liu set his abacus down, studying her. "Well, aren't you a sharp one... Say, how about you come work in my shop?"
"How much monthly pay are we talking?"
The bystanders burst into laughter. Manager Liu chuckled too, tapping her playfully with his fan. "Alright, little boss, off you go. Don't cause trouble for my business."

Amused, Suisui fanned herself and strolled over to the neighboring herb stall. Out of curiosity, she asked the owner why they didn't use the land routes for faster transportation.

"Land routes are faster, but they're bumpy," the stall owner explained patiently. "Herbs can't take a bruising. If they crumble into dust along the road, they aren't worth a copper."

Suisui picked up a herb, sniffed it, and carefully set it back down. "Seven days by water, three days by land. But a bruised cargo loses more than half its value, so trading time for preservation is the smarter investment." She ran the calculations through her head, finding the logic of trade absolutely interesting.

The sun gradually dipped below the horizon, and the crowds along the riverbank began to thin. The last few cargo ships untied their moorings, their sails billowing in the evening breeze as their long shadows drifted across the gold-dusted water. Suisui sat on the stone steps and finally put her fan down. She tilted her head back, tracking the vessels as they cleared the shallows, crossed the heart of the river, and shrank into dark speckles against the edge of the sky.

"Where are they heading...?"

No one replied, but she already knew the answer. Those ships carried grain, fabrics, and herbs gathered from everywhere—the north, the south, the mountains, and the coasts. They would cut through great rivers and scale mountain ranges to reach places far away, where she had never even seen.

"One day, I'll be on one of those ships. Standing at the bow, with the shipping list in my hands."

Before the darkness fully set in, Suisui stood up and brushed the dust from her skirt. The stone steps still held a lingering warmth from the afternoon sun. She turned back to look at the river one last time. Beneath the vast shroud of night, scattered lanterns dotted the dark water like stars. It was breathtakingly beautiful—a world at peace, and a life she loved with all her heart.

When autumn arrived in Minting, the wind swept withered yellow leaves against the latticed window before tearing them away, like someone slowly turning the pages of an old book.

Yangyang was leaving for Jinzhou to become an Outrider. The decision had been made half a month ago. Though the family left it unsaid, everyone kept endlessly busy, as if trying to outrun her departure. Inside the room, Suisui was helping her sister pack. The camphorwood chest had been open all day, the dried mugwort at the bottom releasing a bitter, clean scent. She shook out Yangyang's clothes one by one, folding them with care. Outside, a lone insect chirped in fits and starts, reluctant to surrender to the autumn.

The sunlight carrying the camphorwood's fragrance fell gently across Suisui's hand. Looking up, her gaze rested on the central pillar of the hall. Row upon row of notches were carved into the wood, stretching from knee-height to her ear. The lowest two belonged to Yangyang at ages seven and nine, marked lightly by their father in fear of hurting his daughter. Suisui remembered Yangyang could barely stand straight back then, leaning against the pillar for support. Yet, even as a toddler, she had been exceptionally sweet, filling Suisui's heart with a silent pride: Yes, this is my beloved little sister.

Further up was Suisui's own notch from when she was fourteen, a year she had thrown a tantrum to leave home and study medicine. Her father hadn't refused and simply made her stand before this pillar for half a day. Staring at the stacked markings, she had watched herself grow, inch by inch. Somehow, she realized her growth felt both so fast and so slow—she had grown tall, yet she still had so much to learn.

Near the top, Yangyang's notches grew closer together. The one from last winter, carved by Yangyang herself, was barely half a finger shorter than Suisui's. By spring, they stood at the exact same height.
A scattering of birdsong drifted from the courtyard. Suisui pushed the door open, the autumn sun striking her face with a fleeting warmth. Beneath the eaves, a blue-backed bird leaped from a branch, shaking down a rustle of yellow leaves.

Yangyang was crossing the yard. Pausing at the steps, she saw her older sister under the veranda and walked over. Suisui offered a soft smile.
"When do you set off?"
"Tomorrow morning."
Suisui let out a quiet "Oh." She wanted to say more, but the words dissolved on her tongue. Instead, she reached out and gently adjusted the collar of Yangyang's cloak. Yangyang stood perfectly still, waiting. Only when Suisui pulled her hands away did Yangyang speak in a low voice: "I will come back."
Suisui smiled. "Go on, then. The winds are harsh in Jinzhou. Take care of yourself."
Yangyang nodded. Hearing their parents call her name, she turned to join them. She walked slowly, her back held straight, already adapting to the bearing of an Outrider.

Once more, Suisui was left alone. The blue-backed bird returned to its branch, chirping with its head tilted high. Withered leaves blanketed the steps. She bent down to pick one up, wondering which book she should press it into, before realizing it didn't really matter.

After all, autumn always passes.

Suisui stood up. From far beyond the walls, the distant neighing of a horse drifted in, sounding like an echo from Jinzhou. She knew it was impossible, yet she stood listening for a long time before turning back to the room.

The camphor chest was still open, waiting for her to close it.

Winter in Mengzhou rarely brought snow, but that year, a soft white blanketed the lake in just half a day. The boatman rowed slowly, tactfully keeping silent so as not to disturb it.

Suisui sat at the bow, a white porcelain pot resting on her lap. The steam rising from its spout dispersed the moment it hit the chilly air. She poured a cup for her guest, then filled her own. The faint splash of tea hitting the porcelain was quiet, yet it easily masked the sound of the oars cutting through the water.

The negotiation was going poorly. The opposing party refused to yield, and the stalemate had dragged on for three days. That morning, Suisui had sent an invitation, suggesting they set the matter aside and meet on the lake. The guest arrived fashionably late, wrapped in a gray cloak as the sun began to dip into the west, offering only a brief nod as she boarded.

The small boat drifted toward the center of the lake. A light mist rolled across the water, slowly dissolving the silhouettes of the distant mountains. In such a rare, tranquil setting, Suisui naturally put the business deal aside. Always sharp and eloquent, she broke the ice by speaking of her hometown. She described its waters, so clear one could count every mismatched pebble at the bottom. She spoke of her childhood, watching merchant caravans unload on the riverbank, the stacked sacks towering feet above her head while the crisp, enchanting clatter of abacus beads echoed through the air. She painted a picture of the day she left home under a drizzling rain, where the misty rain blurred even the faces of her parents sending her off. These distant stories traveled across the years aboard their swaying skiff, arriving at last upon this snow-dusted lake in Mengzhou.

"For me, the more of this world I see, the more I fall in love with it," Suisui murmured. "I want good things to reach the places they belong. Grain to famine-stricken lands, medicine to the sickbed, fabrics to the impoverished. But these things won't walk to those in need on their own. Someone has to connect the dots, and I don't want to just be a bystander."

The guest didn't answer, only rested her teacup against her knee and gazed out over the water. Suisui watched her fingers tighten and loosen against the rim of the cup, before a faint sigh finally escaped her lips.

By the time the boat docked, the snow had grown heavier, falling like delicate flakes of cotton. Stepping onto the stone stairs, the guest looked back at her and finally uttered the words: "We will talk again tomorrow." Then, raising her umbrella, she vanished into the snowstorm. Watching the gray silhouette fade into the white expanse, Suisui knew the tide had turned.

Suisui stood by the shore for a long time before leaving. Her lodgings lay to the east of the lake, and by the time she walked through the door, her shoes were soaked through. She knelt before the hearth to start a fire. Sparks sputtered a few times before catching, and the charcoal's warmth seeped outward, first comforting the back of her hands, then warming her face. As the snow fell silently outside the window, she leaned against the hearth, her eyelids growing heavy.

In her dream, it was summer in her hometown. The sun was blindingly bright, and the indoor air baked out a rich fragrance of aged timber. Caravans were unloading tea bricks, dockworkers shouldered heavy sacks of salt, and the shopkeeper tossed strings of copper coins onto the counter with a rhythmic chime that sounded sweeter than any music.

Barely reaching an adult's waist, little Suisui stood beneath the window of the counting house. Peeking over the ledge on her tiptoes, she was utterly transfixed, ignoring anyone who called her name as her eyes shone with brilliant focus.

Back then, she didn't understand the mechanics of commerce. She only knew that the most fascinating things in the world lived within that small window frame. The merchant looked up, caught her staring, and smiled. Reaching into his brush pot, he slid an old paintbrush out through the window. Suisui reached to take it. The brush was thicker than her fingers and felt immensely heavy in her hand. Gripping it tightly, she slowly stood tall beneath the window.

Suddenly, the clinking of copper coins, the jingle of mule bells, the shouting of vendors, and the rhythmic chants of the dockworkers all rushed toward her, enveloping her small frame. She smiled, her eyes crinkling into crescents, filled to the brim with overflowing joy.

Nightfall descended upon the Land of Xuanfang, the twilight sinking inch by inch across the horizon. Suisui walked along the thoroughfare, her steps clicking softly against teal stone slabs. The sky's amber afterglow bathed the street where unlit lanterns swayed beneath the eaves. Shops were closing for the night. Vendors carried wooden shutter boards back and forth, their casual chatter drifting into the evening air. Suisui moved through the shifting shadows, her silhouette stretching long across the ground.

The Waking Moon Festival was drawing near. Stacks of colorful silk lined the storefronts as owners counted the bolts being carried inside. A group of children dashed past her, only to freeze at the street corner. They stared wide-eyed at a row of steaming mechanical cauldrons, swallowing hard before finally tearing themselves away with reluctant backward glances.

Suisui stopped by the stall and observed for a while. The vendor was selling "Brocade Pearl Meatballs"—glistening, tender meatballs garnished with green onions, lined up neatly inside a bamboo steamer.

"A steamer of Brocade Pearl Meatballs, please."
The vendor cheerfully packed her order. Taking the warm pouch, Suisui paid her tab, then slid a few extra Shell Credits across the counter.
"For those children who just ran past. Please give them each one," she said, her voice light as she turned to leave. "No need to tell them who it's from."
The vendor blinked in surprise, but by the time he looked up, her figure had already vanished into the crowd.

As darkness set in, lanterns across teahouses and taverns flickered to life, spilling warm, golden light onto the pavement. Suisui stepped through the glowing patches, her hands full with the bag of warm meatballs. When the wind blew a stray lock of hair across her face, she didn't even have a spare hand to brush it away.

She suddenly realized she had left her water fan behind. She chuckled, unbothered. There were few occasions that truly required her to wield it anyway. The real storm had already been weathered during the Siege of Xuanfang Hold. Everything had settled now, peaceful enough that she had the luxury to stroll the streets and watch people spend a perfectly commonplace evening.

With that thought, her pace unconsciously quickened.

Just past the narrow alley and over a small bridge lay her destination. Her sister was there, and so was that person. She wondered if they had already lit the lamps, and whether they would enjoy this dish. She had walked through the spring and summer of Mingting, where her young self ran through bustling crowds with her hair flying in the wind, her heart captivated by the vibrant tapestry of the world. She had walked through the autumn and winter of Mengzhou, rowing into misty mornings to negotiate trade, and sitting alone on snowy nights to read family letters over and over by the hearth.

And now, those seasons had led her to this very evening. Beneath her feet was the path of Xuanfang. In her hands was a treat for the people she cherished. Suisui shifted the pouch to her other hand, her strides growing faster. As the wind rushing from the end of the street set her sleeves fluttering against the hazy glow of the city lights, she squinted into the brightness, her steps never faltering.

The bridge was just ahead.

Three days had passed since she told her mother of her ambition.
That evening, an extra pair of chopsticks sat at the family's table.
"I hear your child wants to join the military? Which one is it?" Over after-dinner talk, the guest sipped her tea and put the question to her parents.
"Mm... clear eyes, a pure heart. The sort who can endure hardship." The guest studied that still-childish face and smiled. "Seems you have some grounding already. Where did you learn it? A kwoon? They teach no true craft there. If you want to take the field against an enemy, what they teach is not enough."
"Come, show me what you've learned so far." The guest rose and stepped down into the courtyard. "I can't enjoy your mother's cooking for free."
"All right." With her parents' nod, she drew out the wooden sword she used for daily practice, came before the guest, and took her stance.
Who the guest was, she didn't know, only that she was a friend of her parents. But sharp as she was, Yangyang understood why the woman had come to dinner that night, and why she'd offered to test her.
Her parents stood behind her wish, but they would have her see, too, how many trials still lay between her and its fulfillment.
She threw herself at her first trial, like a fledgling beating its wings for the first time, reaching for the open sky.
...
"Good spirit. A shame your talent is ordinary, nothing like those one-in-ten-thousand prodigies. On the path of the martial arts, you could give your whole life and still never reach the end."
The instant she sank to the ground, she felt as though she'd returned to her very first day at the kwoon.
Knowing nothing. Lost and adrift.
"Your mother's spoken to me of your other gifts. Take up her craft instead, and I have no doubt you would surpass her in no time." The guest picked up the wooden sword she'd dropped. "Even so, do you still want to keep on?"
She nodded, reached out, and gripped the hilt held out to her.
...
After that, every dozen days or so the guest would call at Yangyang's home, and never left without offering Yangyang a pointer or two, now of swordplay, now of strategy. She wouldn't let Yangyang call her "Master," insisting she was only a guest cadging meals, driven by some strange shim to tutor a friend's child.
"If I may ask... when will I know that I'm ready?"
"Hmm... let's do it this way."
The next morning, a wooden post stood in Yangyang's yard. Black-gray through and through, its surface hard as iron. Even a real blade would struggle to leave a mark.
The guest took up Yangyang's wooden sword and swung it lightly. A fierce gust passed, and the blade had bitten three inches deep.
She pointed to the deep gash. "When you can do the same without your Resonance Ability, you'll be ready."
...
The seasons fled. Two years went by.
The girl's face had shed its childhood softness, and the post bore cuts beyond counting, deep and shallow alike.
She held her breath and squared her stance. The flash of the blade was like wind, lifting a carpet of leaves from the ground.
"..."
The stroke, freighted with two years of perseverance, sank scarcely a tenth of an inch past the surface.
Today was the day she'd agreed with her parents to leave home for Jinzhou.
She hadn't met the mark her "Master" had set before setting out, but set out she did.
She bowed deeply to the post and left the wooden sword behind in the courtyard.
After farewells to her parents and sister, she walked past Mingting's walls. Just as she was about to pass the first checkpoint, she caught sight of a figure in the distance.
"Forgive, Master. I failed."
"And what if I told you that you might never do it, not in a lifetime of trying?"
"Then I think... I'd grieve a little while."
"But that would not stop you, would it?"
"No."
"Good." The "Master" patted her head and turned away toward the city. "Know that this world holds things you'll never be able to do, and then..."
"...walk on, all the way."

The walk from <te href=260009>Mingting</te> to <te href=850091>Jinzhou</te> cost her a long, long time, long enough to feel like a lifetime apart, long enough that everything she witnessed and endured along the way could shatter everything she'd thought she had built within herself.
She once believed she had glimpsed the "truth." She once believed she knew, clear as day, for whom her sword should be raised. That she could weigh "right" against "wrong," tell "good" from "evil." That a measure lived in her heart. But the more places she walked, the more she found that measure could not be taken to everything in the world.
Some held pure goodwill at the start of their paths, yet had everything ended in tragedy. Some were steeped in sin, yet sheltered the happiness of others with that very evil. The world was too intricate, so intricate that a whole life might not be enough to fathom it.
And then there came a time when she let go even of fathoming.
It was in Yuezhou. A mother had begged her help in finding the child stolen from her.
The ones who took the child were a local faction that worshipped an evil god, a pack of maniacs whose hands were drenched in sin, creatures no longer fit for the word "human."
When she stormed their stronghold alongside the local <te href=260010>Ministry of War</te>, what met her eyes was the very definition of hell
In that moment, every thought burned away in her mind. All that was good and fair, she flung far behind her.
...
It was only when the soldiers of the Ministry of War had finished clearing the field and clapped her shoulder that she realized it was over.
She heard a faltering drip, falling from her the tip of her sword where it bit the earth. Unbinding her hair, she found the ribbon her mother had given her soaked in a red too stark to bear.
She couldn't clearly recall what passed in that stretch of time. Had she taken a life? And if not this time, then so long as she walked this road, the day would come.
She knew that if she would not face so plain a truth, her sword would hold no true strength.
Still, the taste of it was bitter.
Setting out again, she washed her ribbon clean of its stain, but not the gloom from her eyes.
Even with that mother's heartfelt thanks, even having guarded the joy of the innocent, she couldn't return them a single honest smile.
Carrying that broken heart, she came alone into Jinzhou, and stood at the heart of a square that looked out toward the City Hall. She knew where she ought to go next, but her feet felt cast in lead, and she could not bring herself to take that one step.
...
"Hey—why're you standing here by yourself? Are you lost or something?"
"I'm Chixia, a Jinzhou Patroller—well, 'trainee' Patroller. Anything I can help with, just say the word! Oh right, are you hungry? Listen, when you're in Jinzhou you have to try Panhua's Restaurant..."
...Until a frank, easy girl her own age struck up a word with her. Until that girl took her hand and pulled her off toward all that she hadn't had the chance to know.

Yangyang, this is Baizhi, a researcher from <te href=850092>Huaxu Academy</te>. During your evaluation, she'll be providing technical support while you look into the newly formed <te href=850078>Tacet Field</te> near <te href=850091>Jinzhou</te>.
...
"Greetings. My name is Baizhi..."
"—Yangyang! What's for lunch today? Auntie called us over to try a new dish she made. Oh, but those Wuthercakes we had together last time were..."
"Pardon me, but the investigation begins this afternoon. I'm afraid there won't be time for the two of you to eat."
"Even an army marches on food. Whatever it is, it can wait till after we've eaten... and, uh, who are you...?"
"..."
That day, when those verdant eyes met the flame-red pupils for the first time, the very same thought likely rose in both their minds at once: "There's no way I'll ever get along with this person."
"Haha..." Two utterly different temperatures flanked her on either side, and yet, strangely, she felt neither awkward nor ill at ease.
It was as if she had known all along this meeting would come; as if it was written that the three of them should come to know one another just this way.
Tense as the air between them was, she thought, they were still looking at each other.
"Well then. Let's buy something to take along and eat on the way." She clapped her hands lightly and offered a middle path. "Baizhi, fieldwork takes stamina too. You can't head out on an empty stomach."
"Mm... a fair suggestion."
"Then let's try that place that opened last week... No. Yangyang, you decide."
That was the first time the three figures—blue, white, and red—walked side by side down the streets of Jinzhou.
...
"Yangyang, this is a new remedy Huaxu has just developed. Take it to Chixia, would you? A dose of this and her cold will clear up in a day or two."
"I can, of course. But Baizhi, won't you bring it to her yourself?"
"Mm..."
...
"Oh, Yangyang, Auntie Panhua fried up some dishes. Take them along. Isn't Baizhi working late tonight? These can be her midnight snack."
"I can, sure... but Chixia, you could bring them to her yourself, you know."
"Uh..."
...
And so the days went by, one after another. No memories cut to the bone, no dramatic turns like something out of a play.
Across countless days, plain as water, they came slowly to know one another, by ways direct and indirect.
"Baizhi, about the investigation coming up... Chixia happens to know that terrain well, so I made a point of asking the <te href=850089>Patrol Station</te> to lend her to us for a while."
"Ahem... for Yangyang's sake, that is. With me leading the way, nobody has to run all over the place, and the job goes quicker too..."
"Understood..." Baizhi closed the file in her hands and shut her eyes a moment in thought. "So then..."
"...What's for lunch today?"

Ta-da! Yangyang, congratulations on becoming an <te href=850139>Outrider</te>! Baizhi and I picked this out together. Do you like it?
"You'll find yourself often roughing it in the wild being an Outrider, and your hair's a handful to manage. This hat should keep some of the wind and rain off. I think you'll find it quite practical."
"None of that matters, not a bit. What matters is—Yangyang's going to look lovely wearing it, right?"
"Thank you... Baizhi, Chixia."
She took the gift from her friends' hands and put it on her head.
And in that instant, she felt like reliving a scene many years ago.
...
"...What is it, Yangyang?" At a temple fair ablaze with lanterns, her sister noticed her halted before a stall, gazing spellbound at something on the shelves. "Ah, is it that hat you want? Mm... not bad at all! Look, look, it's even got a little bird stitched on it."
"But it's so expensive..." She glanced at the price on the shelf, looked down at the coins clutched in her hand, and edged back a step. "Come on, sister. We said we'd go buy maltose candy together..."
"Mm! Knew it'd look great!" Before she could even come to herself, the hat was already sitting on her head.
"Sister...?! You can't just take what isn't yours..." She fluttered for a moment, then saw Suisui draw a pouch from who knows where and dangle it before her eyes.
"Hehe. Yangyang, you've got no idea how deep your big sister's pockets run." Suisui grinned slyly, coins jingling in the pouch. "It's just one hat. To my little treasury, that's a drop in the bucket."
"But that's money you worked so hard for..."
"Oh, what's the harm!" Suisui caught her hand and pulled her off toward the livelier stalls. "I'm your big sister! What's mine is yours, and what's yours is mine too, of course..."
...
To her, from the very moment of her birth, having a "big sister" was simply something she took for granted.
She took for granted the laughter and the roughhousing together. She took for granted the sharing of every little thing. She took for granted... her constant presence in each day of her life.
Not until she made that decision did she realize she was about to bid farewell to everything she'd once taken for granted.
If she didn't take that step, she could never become the "self" she longed to be. And if she did take it, every bond she knew and leaned on must be remade into something new.
She sealed everything about her sister away in her home in <te href=260009>Mingting</te>. And one day, perhaps, when the time came to leave <te href=850091>Jinzhou</te>, she'd seal away everything in this place too?
She didn't know. But she did know that...
...Right here, right now, the warmth coming down from atop her head was no different from all those years ago.
She knew she was no longer the little girl who'd run after her sister through the temple fair.
She knew her sister's next letter would arrive next month.

That encounter, that day... Was it chance? Or was it fate? When you first awoke, you had forgotten everything. Yet those golden eyes of yours tell me that what you carry, what you've lived through, may reach far beyond anything I can imagine. You always rush to the front of everyone without hesitation. You're always set on putting yourself at the eye of the storm. Is that a choice you make? Or has it already become instinct? You always... take a bigger step than the rest. And no matter how many once walked at your side, you always... end up where none of us can follow. But I don't believe there's any such thing as a soul fated to be alone. Maybe I only want to do this for my own sake. I just want to protect someone... well... someone who knows so little about protecting {Male=himself;Female=herself}. Though the time we shared may be, against the whole of your journey, no more than a single wave on a boundless sea. Still, this feeling, this impulse... It has nothing to do with worthiness or with time. It's simply my own... extravagant wish. I hope that, in joy or in sorrow, through fair days or foul, when you need someone to lean on, when you need someone to confide in, I can be standing at your side. I hope... ... Her pen tip came to a stop. She stared at the half-written letter, reading it over, silently, again and again. In the end, she folded the sheet, slipped it into an envelope, and tucked it away beneath her drawer. She drew out a fresh sheet and began to write again. Rover, how have you been lately? Is everything going well?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en:
The clouds hang heavy with coming rain, and mist rises from the water... See? What do you make of the dewy sights today? When I do business in <te href=850154>Mengzhou</te>, I see weather like this often. A touch different from Xuanfang Hold, and nothing at all like the views in my hometown... 

Perhaps each rainfall in this world has its own little temper. But it was this very drizzle splashing on teal stone slabs today that also fell on me decades ago. I heard its voice calling to me. And ever since, water has followed my will. It flows or rests at my command. And when I pluck the air just so, it comes to me, like an old friend. 

Now I walk in the rain with no need for parasol or shelter. The raindrops know me, and I know them.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Speaking of hometowns, my mind wanders back to my childhood in <te href=260009>Mingting</te>. Everything felt so impossibly soothing in the March spring breeze—the high grass, the soaring birds, and each dawn less heavy than the last. I often dragged Yangyang out to fly kites. I can still feel the exact moment the wind would catch them, the line snapping taut as if we'd actually hooked a cloud. To ensure my kite soared higher than everyone else's, I'd run as fast as I could.\n\nThe courtyard was filled with the chatter of birds, the susurrus of leaves, and the sunlight... Oh, how it filtered through the branches like shattered gold, dusting everything it touched. Even after all these years, that remains the most beautiful thing I've ever seen.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Springs back then—the wind oh so soft, the sky oh so blue, and a qin's melody oh so occasionally drifting over the courtyard wall. Our house never wanted for music. From dawn till dusk, it lilted through every hall and corner, enveloping me like running water. My parents, bless them, always knew I lacked the patience to sit at the qin and practice my technique. Yangyang, though, was my opposite. Even as a child, she could sit through an entire piece in perfect silence, her little hands tapping the rhythm against her knees with a solemn focus beyond her years. But me? I loved to slip away to some open ground and simply dance. A light tap of the foot, a swirl of the sleeves, and a well-timed gust of wind... In those moments it felt as if I could gather the very brilliance of nature into my arms. There was nothing more enjoyable than that.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Beyond our courtyard lay an entirely different world. I was drawn to the docks, to the groan of ropes biting into wooden pilings as freighters moored, the shouts of vendors, and the rhythmic clack of abacus beads. To me, those sounds were more enchanting than any melody. I would crouch by the stalls and peer at ledgers, balancing accounts that weren't mine to balance or spreading out maps to correct a traveler's route. "This path is too long," I'd insist. "The river will save you two days." At first, the adults laughed it off as a child's game, until they realized I was right. My mother later joked to my father that perhaps their little girl had a natural gift for trade...\nWell, what do you think?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en:
At first, I only saw the bustle, the lovely noise of it all. It was only later that I came to see that "peace and prosperity" aren't a given. They're fragile things, held together only by those who tend them. I decided then to be such a person.

I love this land, but I love the life humming within it even more. I could never settle for the safety of a quiet corner while others struggle. Still, I know the limits of one person's strength. I have seen villages hollowed by disaster and people who have lost their homes—the kind of wounds that no shipment of supplies can ever quite heal. These are realities I simply cannot change alone.

Tell me... if the day comes to stake everything on the future of this land, will there be someone to help me weave the vision I see? What I want is a world alive and thriving, and in you, I see the possibility of making that real.

So, if you're willing... take this path with me.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Heh... the list grows longer by the day, I'm afraid. Lately, I've been quite obsessed with antiques and paintings. Even the little imitations from street stalls are fascinating in their own way, you know. There are certain tricks of the trade you only truly appreciate once you see them firsthand. I've even tried my hand at a few sketches. They're quite decent, if I do say so myself... Want to have a look?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: My troubles...? Money handles most of them quite tidily, thank goodness. All but one, that is: what to do now that my sister has grown up? Argh... when did she decide she didn't need me to hold her hand anymore?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Pastries, of course! Everything from the delicate pea flour cakes to those red bean rolls wrapped in white kidney bean paste. And then there are the soft, pillowy rice balls. Sweet without being cloying, simply melting on the tongue. I've also grown fond of the "Little Snowy Moons" here in Mengzhou. They have this wonderful, subtle aroma within that chewy cake texture, entirely different from the flavors back home. One day, I really must bring some back for my family to try.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Despite my time in <te href=850154>Mengzhou</te>, I still can't stomach the pickled local fare. It's a tragedy, truly. I'll see a dish that looks absolutely exquisite, translucent and perfectly plated, only to find I can't bring myself to take a bite. It's enough to make a grown woman sigh.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: I want wealth that knows no border. I want goods to find their way, people to find their place. I want the warm light of every home burning, always burning, forever.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Dumpling, over here! See? Isn't she a delight? Dumpling has a marvelous affinity for water. She whirls and chirps around me whenever I use my Forte to bend the currents... Mm, that's all it takes to make this little birdie happy.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: My family always let me do as I pleased, but choosing the way of the merchant was never a simple impulse. It began with watching and learning—observing how the street vendors set their rules and negotiated their deals before I ever dared to try it myself.\n\nOh, to watch the figures on a ledger slowly change, trade routes rise from nothing, and the cargo passing through my hands become the grain, fabric, or medicine that keeps another soul alive... That, my dear, is worth more than all the gold in the world. Commerce, you see, is not about calculation. It's about making a way for people to live.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Since we were children, people have said that Yangyang and I share only a face, that our spirits couldn't be more different. I was the one who needed to see everything the world had to offer, while she was the quiet, gentle center who kept her thoughts close. Over time, people even joked, asking if we were truly sisters at all.\n\nNeither of us ever took offense. We knew that in all this wide world, you could never find two souls more alike. My sister may look soft and unassuming, but there is a resilience in her that runs deeper than anyone realizes. When you need the wind, she brings it to you. When you face the gale, she stands as your shield. This, I've always known.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Unlike the other <te href=850083>Sentinel</te>s of <te href=850093>Huanglong</te>, Hsin doesn't feel like a divinity looking down from on high. Somehow, I see a part of her that's unmistakably "human." Maybe it's because I know how much she loves this mortal world that I dared to stand before her.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: One of my merchant caravans once spoke of a Transcendent who killed the Tacet Discords blocking their path through Xuanfang. That was Paragon Qingxiao. Between that debt and the support she provided during the Hold's defense, I felt it only right to thank her in person. With proper gifts, of course. But she wouldn't accept a thing. She only sat for a few cups of the tea I brewed. Wait, a tea favored by a famed Transcendent... Now that could be quite the selling point, no?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: The Cat of the Nether Lamp… the rumors make him sound like a ghost story. A figure in black, drifting through shadows with a Nether Lamp and the chill of the netherworld clinging to him. I've only met him a few times. Despite his youth, his eyes have the look of someone who has weathered storms that would break lesser men. He is utterly uninhibited, and it makes me curious: is there anything in this world that could actually hold him back?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: People know her as a master composer, but to me, she remains that gentle presence on the porch, pulling my sister and me into her arms on rainy days to tell us stories of the world beyond. I was always pressing her for what came next, while Yangyang would just watch her in quiet, wide-eyed wonder. Hehe, I suppose that was the rhythm of our childhood.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: You couldn't find a more open-minded man in this world than my father. A teacher by trade, but never, ever the lecturing sort. He has a gift for tossing out witty lines with such ease that even the dullest classics become engrossing tales. I always laugh out loud over his letters. He writes with such flair that events happening a thousand miles away become just next door's news in his hands. You'll just have to see for yourself when you visit our home in <te href=260009>Mingting</te> someday. Beautiful views, and I promise, the best tea you'll ever taste.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en:
Today is your birthday. Oh, naturally, I've had it marked.

I thought about organizing a grand banquet for you, the kind where the table bends under all those dishes and nobody is allowed to leave. But then it occurred to me that sort of merrymaking can be arranged anytime. Today, you should follow your own heart. Whether that means a lively crowd or a quiet corner with no one to disturb you, I'll make sure you get it. On a day like this, you're allowed to be a little selfish.

I'm a terribly "greedy" creature, I admit. I believe the best days ought to be savored slowly, and the sweetest meetings enjoyed long after the party ends. The world is vast and time is long. Whether you want a hall full of delicacies or just a quiet cup of tea, you need only ask me.

May every year be as bright as today. May you always follow your heart, and may every road you walk lead to the light.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Watch closely, Dumpling... See? Quite lifelike, isn't it?

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: May peace and plenty bless this land for good.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: If this isn't enough to pave the way, then let the rivers and mountains be the proof of what I'm willing to wager.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Where clear streams flow, there spring awaits.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: This ensemble... rather interesting, I must say.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: The sound of water... I hear it. Not from the streams, or the falling rain, but from somewhere far deeper. A resonance that seeps from the core of every living thing, waking the hills, waking the waters, one by one.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: In the misty rains of Mengzhou, most people reach for their oil-paper umbrellas or scurry under the nearest eaves. But I don't mind the wet. I stroll leisurely through the rain while the droplets simply curve around my shoulders and drift away to find somewhere else to fall.... So stay close to me, darling. We've no use for umbrellas here.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: I think the most precious thing in this world is the light that meets your eyes the moment you raise them. The first break of dawn, the river's surface glistening with flecks of gold, as fishing boats drift in small clusters to the rhythmic creak of oars. Then the markets stir. Bamboo lids lift, unfurling white breaths of steam carrying the scent of fresh buns. It mingles with the teahouses' distant melodies and the laughter of children at play... I don't just hear these sounds now. I feel the pulse behind them. A pulse threading together to form a rich tapestry that I cannot bear to lose.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: People speak of commerce as if it's just buying and selling. But if you look closer, every trade route ends at someone's front door. Grain from the north. Tea from the south. Herbs from the mountains. Fabrics from the shores. Someone has to thread it all together, like a needle pulling a string, mending one land's scarcity with another's abundance.\n\nThese quiet exchanges are what have kept the world moving for generations. Water can wear down stone, or it can nourish a garden. Commerce can chase profit, or it can save a world. This is the path I've chosen.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: The mountains and rivers are like a painting come to life. And this world, this bustling, breathing world, is so vibrant... but to witness it alone is a lonely thing. So... let's see the rest of it together. How big this world is, with its boundless wonders patiently waiting. For you. For me.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Mirrored by water, tinted in blue.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Beyond lush haze, the rainfall marches.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: That... I'll mark on my ledger.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: The world's sweet noise... I wanted more.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Such beauty... so too must it end.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: This path... I'll walk no further.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Come now. I could use another dancer.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Any new tricks? Do impress me.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: World's warm breath, in my sight.

speaker: Suisui
anh_en: Seems the scales tipped my way, hm?

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: ...I thought that when I saw you again, words would come pouring out—so many that I wouldn't know where to start. But... now that you're really here, my heart is so full of joy that it pushed everything else away.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: A lot has happened in Jinzhou while you were away. I've written to you about the long and short of it. Yet, some stories are just better told face to face, right? So, the adventures you mentioned in your letters—the Black Shores, Ragunna, , and Lahai-Roi—would you share them with me again?

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: The role of a Xuan Watcher... Though it's only a temporary undertaking, I'm still orienting myself. Sometimes I catch myself worrying about Jinzhou. But Chixia, Baizhi, <te href=850118>Magistrate Jinhsi</te>, and General Jiyan... these names bring peace just at their mentioning. I hope that one day, my name can bring that same reassurance to others.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: The night before I left for Xuanfang Hold, I had a nightmare... In it, I was searching for a person... someone I'd never actually met. It wasn't until I woke up that I realized that person was you. But like what you said in your letter—a dream is only a dream. Now that I can see you, touch you, and feel you... I don't think I'll ever have a dream like that again.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: I know that after this reunion, the time will come for us to part again. But this time, our shared memories are the stories we lived, we didn't have to reduce them to words in letters. And, through the bittersweetness of our parting, our next meeting may be all the more worth looking forward to... Who knows? Maybe next time, I'll be the one coming to see you.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: My sister used to take me kite-flying all the time. She'd joke that as long as I was there, we could catch a breeze even on a windless day. But when we were competing to see whose kite flew higher, she'd watch me like a hawk to make sure I didn't cheat—not that she'd stand a chance catching me if I did.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: I've crossed paths with all kinds of people on this journey. Some walked with me, some passed me by, and some... drew the line against me. With them, there was no middle ground nor room for compromises, no matter how much of ourselves we shared. I know there will be more of this kind the further down this path. But it won't stop me from moving forward. My ideals and faith have forged the blade I carry. It protects at the same time as it cuts... Should the day come when I must point it at others... my resolve was made long ago.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: My mother's cooking... My sister and I both love it. Though neither of us can say we love it as much as Father does. After all, it was her cooking that captured my father's... Ahem—if you're curious about its taste, {PlayerName}, I could try my hand at it. I haven't quite mastered her touch yet, but... I'd probably improve faster with a good taste tester.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: Food I dislike? Hm... I'm not a picky eater. But when it comes down to it... eating alone makes the heartiest meal taste bland.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: Protection takes many forms. It can be stepping up for the defenseless, lifting someone out of hardship, or simply offering a quiet ear for someone who's hurting. But whatever the case may be, you must be strong enough to support others. That is why I must press on along my path. I don't dream of gaining the power to protect the world, but for now... I want to stand by your side. Together, I believe we can protect so much more.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: The sword once enshrined in Xianling Village... I didn't realize until the very end that it carried a faint trace of a Xuanling Bird's frequency. Their last songs were echoes of agony and grief. But I can sense the undercurrent of love and longing layered within. It's a melody intricately woven with many sounds, a tribute to life.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: I had never been to <te href=270001>Xuanfang</te> before, and yet... the Streams here feel strangely familiar. After learning the legend of the Xuanling Birds, I've started to sense their presence in the Streams... If only they still existed in the world—no, call it a hunch, but I know they shall re-emerge, and one day, the people of Xuanfang will see them soaring through the skies once more.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: My sister... she's always been the pillar of confidence and reliability. I grew up following her footsteps, convinced there was nothing in this world she couldn't handle. She's not perfect—sometimes she goes on her stubborn streaks and lets her temper out. Sometimes, I catch a glimpse of her vulnerable side when she tries to compose herself and she thinks I wouldn't notice. To the world, she wears many masks: the noble lady of a great house, a cunning rival, the resourceful president of the commerce guild. But to me, she is simply my sister.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: <te href=850118>Magistrate Jinhsi</te>... she carries herself with such poise that it masks her age. I wonder if she feels she doesn't measure up to more experienced leaders, or to the person she envisions herself becoming. What she doesn't see is that, to me and to every citizen of Jinzhou she's ever helped, she's already the best Magistrate we could have asked for.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: The Blessed Maiden of Rinascita, a wandering knight... I can see her drifting across the land of Rinascita like untethered winds from here on. You see resemblances between us? Well, our Tacet Marks are both on our foreheads. Though that's probably just a coincidence. We can both transform, too—uh, not in the same way... But when it comes to it, if I could transform into a more "mature" version of myself—Hmm, I don't think I can quite picture that.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: In <te href=270001>Xuanfang</te>, Liangyu has been an immense help to me. Since I'm serving as an acting Xuan Watcher, that technically makes her a senior of mine. She often wears a frown, but once you get to know her, you'll see how deeply she cares for the people she holds dear. Like the spring drizzle that quietly nourishes the land, she gives so much of herself in secret—and she gets so embarrassed whenever anyone finds out.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: My mother... She was once a renowned composer in <te href=850093>Huanglong</te>. Father told me she won a music competition when she was even younger than I am now. These days, she's stepped away from the spotlight to focus on our family. Some people say her talent has faded, but that, of course, is only a rumor. My sister and I grew up surrounded by her compositions. They far outnumber even Father's vast collection of books.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: When I was little, Father always told my sister and me that he was just an ordinary teacher, desiring nothing but an early retirement. It wasn't until much later that I realized what kind of "important figures" his students were... The day I left for <te href=850091>Jinzhou</te>, he gave me a pen. He said that whether I was happy or sad, it was better to write things down than to keep them bottled up inside. He was worried that I wouldn't find someone to confide in while I was away, but fortunately, I found you.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: The Streams... For the longest time, they hadn't been actual voices. But at some point, something changed. A faint, flickering echo emerged, like a distant, dreamlike call. Since then, I've begun to hear so much more, both from the past and the present. I don't know yet what this shift means, but I've braced myself for whatever it brings. The wind has taught and guided me. Perhaps, it comes down to me to search for the final answer. And I believe it lies within the wind.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: Happy birthday to you, happy birthday to you... Happy birthday to you, happy birthday to you... As always, this song is specially for you.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: ...Phew, a long journey starts with a single step.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: Come on! Let's go where the wind takes us.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: Don't worry. Leave it to me.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: I'll learn to master this power as quickly as I can...!

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: Sounds could be weighty. Jadeite could be made light.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: In the surging currents of the Streams, I hear the constant whispering of the name—"Votary of the Voice." Does it refer to me? Or...?

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: These wings will soar across the skies and the wilds, reach shores no one has set foot on before... and build a bridge that channels all voices of the world.

speaker: Yangyang: Xuanling
anh_en: I entrust this feather to you. It's more than a charm—it's my vow. Even if your journey takes you somewhere winds don't blow; even if the Streams no longer carry your voice... As long as you carry it and call my name, I will find my way back to you.
